910.name: Austronesian Origins and Indigenous Cultures
910.description: Taiwan as the probable homeland of all Austronesian peoples, the diverse indigenous Formosan cultures, and the island before European contact — one of the most linguistically diverse places on Earth.

sub_clusters.name: Austronesian Homeland
sub_clusters.description: Taiwan as the origin point of the Austronesian expansion — the largest language family spread by area — from which seafarers colonized Southeast Asia, Oceania, and Madagascar over thousands of years.
key_events: Austronesian peoples begin their epic maritime expansion from Taiwan across the Pacific and Indian Oceans (c. 3000–1500 BC)

sub_clusters.name: Formosan Indigenous Peoples
sub_clusters.description: The sixteen officially recognized indigenous groups of Taiwan, their diverse languages preserving the deepest branches of the Austronesian family, headhunting traditions, and limited Chinese and Japanese contact.
key_events: Taiwan's indigenous languages recognized as preserving the most ancient branches of the Austronesian language family

920.name: European Colonial Period
920.description: The Dutch and Spanish colonial enclaves in Taiwan, Koxinga's dramatic expulsion of the Dutch and establishment of the Kingdom of Tungning, and the Qing conquest.

sub_clusters.name: Dutch and Spanish Formosa
sub_clusters.description: The Dutch East India Company's colony at Fort Zeelandia in southern Taiwan, the Spanish presence in the north at Fort San Domingo, the sugar and deerskin trade, and Christian missionary activities.
key_events: Dutch East India Company establishes Fort Zeelandia — first European colonial government in Taiwan (1624)
Spanish establish Fort San Domingo in northern Taiwan (1626, expelled by Dutch 1642)

sub_clusters.name: Koxinga and Kingdom of Tungning
sub_clusters.description: Zheng Chenggong (Koxinga) expels the Dutch and establishes the Kingdom of Tungning as a Ming loyalist base, the development of Chinese settler agriculture, and the Qing conquest under Shi Lang.
key_events: Koxinga besieges and captures Fort Zeelandia — expelling the Dutch from Taiwan (1662)
Qing Admiral Shi Lang conquers Taiwan — first incorporation into a Chinese empire (1683)

920.name: Qing Dynasty Taiwan
920.description: Taiwan as a frontier prefecture of Fujian Province, waves of Hoklo and Hakka immigration, endemic ethnic violence, the camphor and tea trades, and the brief modernization under Liu Mingchuan.

sub_clusters.name: Frontier Settlement and Ethnic Conflict
sub_clusters.description: The waves of Han Chinese immigration from Fujian and Guangdong, ethnic clashes between Hoklo and Hakka settlers and with indigenous peoples, the 'once every three years a revolt' pattern, and the limited Qing administrative control.
key_events: Lin Shuangwen Rebellion — largest revolt in Qing Taiwan (1786–1788)

sub_clusters.name: Modernization and Japanese Cession
sub_clusters.description: The opening of treaty ports, the tea and camphor export boom, Governor Liu Mingchuan's modernization with Asia's first commercial railway, the Sino-Japanese War, and the cession of Taiwan to Japan.
key_events: Liu Mingchuan builds Taiwan's first railway and installs electric lighting in Taipei (1887–1891)
Treaty of Shimonoseki cedes Taiwan to Japan — Republic of Formosa declared and crushed (1895)

930.name: Japanese Colonial Period
930.description: Fifty years of Japanese colonial rule transforming Taiwan through infrastructure, education, and public health, the suppression of indigenous resistance, the kominka assimilation movement, and wartime mobilization.

sub_clusters.name: Pacification and Colonial Development
sub_clusters.description: The brutal suppression of armed resistance, Governor-General Kodama Gentarō and Gotō Shinpei's modernization programs, sugar industry development, the construction of railways and infrastructure, and the Wushe Incident.
key_events: Wushe Incident — Seediq indigenous people stage armed uprising against Japanese rule (1930)

sub_clusters.name: Kōminka Movement and War
sub_clusters.description: The kōminka (imperialization) policy forcing Japanese names and language, Taiwan as a staging base for the invasion of Southeast Asia, wartime industrial production, and the recruitment of Taiwanese soldiers.
key_events: Japan uses Taiwan as the launching base for the invasion of the Philippines and Southeast Asia (1941–1942)

940.name: Retrocession and White Terror
940.description: The return to Chinese rule, the February 28 Incident, the KMT retreat to Taiwan, martial law, the White Terror period of political repression, and Taiwan's position in the Cold War.

sub_clusters.name: February 28 Incident and KMT Retreat
sub_clusters.description: The handover from Japan, Chen Yi's corrupt administration, the February 28 Incident massacre of thousands, Chiang Kai-shek's retreat to Taiwan with 1.5 million mainlanders, and the declaration of martial law.
key_events: February 28 Incident — KMT troops massacre an estimated 18,000–28,000 Taiwanese (1947)
Chiang Kai-shek retreats to Taiwan with the ROC government and 1.5 million mainlanders (1949)

sub_clusters.name: White Terror and Cold War Ally
sub_clusters.description: The White Terror period with tens of thousands imprisoned or executed, US military protection after the Korean War, land reform, and Taiwan's seat on the UN Security Council representing 'China.'
key_events: US Seventh Fleet deployed to the Taiwan Strait — protecting Taiwan from PRC invasion (1950)
Taiwan loses its UN seat to the People's Republic of China (1971)

940.name: Taiwan Economic Miracle
940.description: Taiwan's transformation into one of the Four Asian Tigers, export-oriented industrialization, the Ten Major Construction Projects, the semiconductor industry's foundation, and the softening of authoritarian rule.

sub_clusters.name: Export-Led Industrialization
sub_clusters.description: The Kaohsiung Export Processing Zone, the Ten Major Construction Projects, the development of the textile and electronics industries, and Taiwan's emergence as an export powerhouse.
key_events: Kaohsiung Export Processing Zone established — pioneering the export zone model (1966)

sub_clusters.name: Technology Revolution and Hsinchu
sub_clusters.description: The establishment of Hsinchu Science Park, the founding of TSMC and UMC, the development of the semiconductor industry that would make Taiwan indispensable to the global economy, and Chiang Ching-kuo's reforms.
key_events: TSMC founded by Morris Chang — would become the world's most important semiconductor company (1987)

950.name: Democratization of Taiwan
950.description: The lifting of martial law after 38 years, the democratic transition, the formation of opposition parties, the first direct presidential election, and the peaceful transfer of power.

sub_clusters.name: End of Martial Law and Transition
sub_clusters.description: Chiang Ching-kuo's lifting of martial law, Lee Teng-hui as the first native Taiwanese president, constitutional reforms, the Wild Lily student movement, and the first direct presidential election.
key_events: Martial law lifted after 38 years — longest period of martial law in modern history (1987)
First direct presidential election — Lee Teng-hui wins amid PRC missile threats (1996)

sub_clusters.name: First Party Transfer and Taiwan Identity
sub_clusters.description: The growth of Taiwanese identity distinct from Chinese identity, the 1999 921 earthquake, and the historic election of DPP candidate Chen Shui-bian ending 55 years of KMT rule.
key_events: Chen Shui-bian wins the presidency — first peaceful transfer of power between parties (2000)

960.name: Contemporary Taiwan and Cross-Strait Relations
960.description: The deepening of democracy, the semiconductor superpower status, the cross-strait tensions with China, Taiwan's COVID-19 success, and the growing international recognition of Taiwan's distinct identity.

sub_clusters.name: Cross-Strait Engagement and Tensions
sub_clusters.description: Chen Shui-bian's independence-leaning presidency, Ma Ying-jeou's rapprochement with Beijing, the ECFA trade agreement, the Sunflower Student Movement against closer ties, and Tsai Ing-wen's election.
key_events: Sunflower Student Movement occupies the Legislative Yuan in protest of trade pact with China (2014)

sub_clusters.name: Silicon Shield and Geopolitical Flashpoint
sub_clusters.description: TSMC's dominance of advanced semiconductor manufacturing, Taiwan as the world's most dangerous geopolitical flashpoint, Pelosi's visit and PRC military exercises, and Taiwan's role in the US-China rivalry.
key_events: TSMC produces over 90% of the world's most advanced semiconductors — the 'Silicon Shield'
Speaker Pelosi visits Taiwan — PRC conducts unprecedented military exercises (August 2022)

unassigned_events.note: Events not yet assigned to a thematic cluster
